$comment: The contract between the training-time pipeline and the app.
This file is the source of truth. tool/vision/export_onnx.py writes graphs
that must satisfy it, tool/vision/verify_contract.py checks that they do,
and lib/data/capture/model_contract.dart mirrors it so the Dart side and
the native bridge agree on tensor names, shapes and class ids without
anyone re-deriving them from a blog post.
The .onnx weights are not in git. They are large binaries produced by the
pinned recipe below and fetched by tool/vision/fetch_models.sh, which
checks them against the digests recorded here.

detector.role: Locates the shooter, the ball, the ring and the backboard.

$comment: BGR, and not by accident: the mmdet RTMDet config sets
bgr_to_rgb=False, so the network was trained on channels in the order
OpenCV loads them, and mean and std are listed in that same order.
The pose model is the opposite (bgr_to_rgb=True, RGB means), so the
two graphs genuinely disagree and a bridge cannot use one channel
order for both. Feeding this one RGB costs roughly twenty pixels of
box centre error, which is small enough to look like a working
detector and large enough to ruin the rim ellipse.

outputs.name: dets
outputs.$comment: x1, y1, x2, y2, score in letterboxed input pixels, score descending.

$classComment: Four classes, not COCO's eighty. COCO has person and sports ball but no
rim and no backboard, and those two are exactly what the calibration
depends on, so the detector is a fine-tune rather than a stock
checkpoint. vision/configs/rtmdet_m_arcvanta.py carries the head change.

pose.role: Body landmarks for the tracked shooter, from the detector's person box.

preprocess.$comment: Top-down: the person box is expanded to the 192x256 aspect ratio, then warped.

decode.$comment: argmax each axis independently, divide by splitRatio for the coordinate in input space, and take the product of the two peak values as the landmark score.

$comment: PoseJoint in lib/data/models/pose.dart is a 14-joint subset. Everything
the product measures is an angle or a displacement between these, so the
face keypoints are dropped at the bridge rather than carried up.
'midpoint' entries are derived, not predicted: COCO has no neck.
Providers are tried in order and the first that loads wins. Both NNAPI
and Core ML silently fall back per-node, so the bridge records which one
actually took the graph and reports it with the session, and a run that
landed on CPU is expected to hold a lower frame rate rather than a
different answer.
